title: The Problem With Perfectionism
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article draws a sharp line between aiming for excellence and demanding perfection, arguing the latter is a self-defeating trap for leaders and performers alike. It explains how perfectionism produces chronic disappointment, frayed nerves, and an inability to enjoy real success, ultimately undermining the very performance it claims to elevate. Citing research showing perfectionists underperform non-perfectionists over time, the piece closes with Winston Churchill's line that "perfectionism spells paralysis," framing challenge and demand as fundamentally different, and only one of them sustainable.
points: Aiming for high standards and demanding perfection are fundamentally different and should not be conflated.
Demanding perfectionism produces chronic disappointment and undermines confidence over time.
Perfectionism creates stress and an inability to enjoy genuine achievements.
Long-running research shows perfectionists are less successful than non-perfectionists across most endeavors.
Challenge energizes people while perfectionism destroys their willingness to take risks.
quotes: The difference between aiming for perfection and demanding it is a chasm leaders must come to terms with.
Leaders and performers who demand perfectionism are guaranteed to be continually disappointed.
Perfectionism is a curse that leaders and performers too often apply on purpose.
Research for more than a century reveals that over time, perfectionists are less successful than non-perfectionists at just about everything.
Winston Churchill almost perfectly described the effects of perfectionism in just three words: “Perfectionism spells paralysis.
